findings.passage: James Talarico walked back into a walkout under fire and capped his own Senate tenure.
findings.problem: The search-snippet description says the opposite of what happened. "Walked back into a walkout" reads as rejoining the walkout, but the body's key scene is that he left the 2021 walkout and returned to the House floor. For a reader who knows nothing about him, this is the first sentence they see, and it misstates the main behavioral evidence. It also leaves out the fact most searchers came for, the November 3, 2026 Senate win.
findings.acceptance_test: A reader who has seen only the description can correctly say that he came back from (did not rejoin) a 2021 Democratic walkout and drew fire from his own party for it. The description stays within 120–170 characters and does not contradict the body or the evidence record.

findings.passage: On August 9, 2021, The Texas Tribune counted at least four House Democrats back on the floor in Austin while most of their caucus stayed in Washington, D.C., holding out against a Republican voting bill.
findings.problem: The hook works as a scene, but an unfamiliar reader is never told why Democrats were in Washington or what returning did. The terms "quorum" and "break quorum" first appear in later sections and are never explained. Unless the reader knows the walkout was meant to deny the House the quorum it needed to pass the bill, the return does not register as costly, and the article's best discriminator ("The 2021 return drew fire from his own caucus") depends on it. The reader also first learns who Talarico is, and that he just won a U.S. Senate seat, in the fifth paragraph.
findings.acceptance_test: By the end of the second paragraph, a reader with no knowledge of Texas politics can explain, in a sourced clause, what the walkout was trying to block and why coming back undercut it. "Quorum" is defined in plain words where it first appears. A one-line identity cue (Texas Democrat, now senator-elect) appears before the reader is asked to judge his motives, and the opening scene stays.

findings.passage: He campaigned to ban super PACs while a super PAC backing him, Lone Star Rising PAC, ran an attack ad against Crockett in the primary.
findings.problem: The 2026 race is never laid out, so three evidence passages are hard to follow. Crockett is introduced only as someone he chose not to attack in a debate. The body never says he won the March primary against her. Colin Allred shows up in the allegation section as someone he "signed up to run against", with no explanation of who Allred is. Cornyn's supporters are described as up for grabs without the article ever saying that Paxton beat Cornyn in the Republican runoff. A new reader cannot judge the super PAC tension or the "mediocre" allegation without knowing who was running against whom, and who won.
findings.acceptance_test: Wherever these figures first appear, a reader can answer from the body alone: who his primary opponents were, that he won the Democratic nomination (with date and source, e.g. S21), and how Paxton became the Republican nominee (only if a source supports it). There should be no new section, just one or two orienting clauses.

findings.passage: The same record includes a classroom story larger than the documents and a campaign that sanded down his sharpest edges.
findings.problem: The intro sets up a classroom story larger than the documents. The next classroom story the reader meets is Justin, in "Two years at Rhodes", which comes with its own caveat that officials "could not confirm the specifics." An unfamiliar reader will reasonably take Justin to be the inflated story. The real referent, the 45-student claim, shows up about 100 lines later in the Type 3 section.
findings.acceptance_test: A first-time reader reaching the end of "Two years at Rhodes" does not confuse the Justin story with the disputed class-size story. Either the intro names the 45-student claim, or the Rhodes section briefly flags that the class-size dispute is covered later.

findings.passage: The same pattern turns his injuries into rules.
findings.problem: Several connectives point back to things the reader has not been given. "The same pattern" follows the Bernal "haunted" paragraph, which describes a feeling, not a pattern of turning wrongs into rules (that pattern is Justin, two paragraphs earlier). "In his telling, his aggression always arrives with a license" comes before the article has shown any aggression. "The same Tribune report notes he then held a competitive suburban seat" sits right after a link to the San Antonio Current copy, so it is unclear which report is meant.
findings.acceptance_test: Each of the three phrases points to something the reader has already seen in the text just before it, and a cold reader can name the antecedent without rereading earlier sections.

findings.passage: He told ABC News he made $600 a month as a legislator and offered to pay the fines himself.
findings.problem: Two details trail off for a new reader. "The fines" have not been introduced (who was fining absent members, and for what?). "A Colbert interview CBS declined to broadcast" raises an obvious question (why?) that the article never answers, so it reads as a teaser with no payoff in a section about attention.
findings.acceptance_test: "The fines" gets a short sourced explanation (or the clause is cut), and the Colbert detail either gets a sourced half-clause of context or loses the "declined to broadcast" hook.

findings.passage: His temperament is where [Type 9](/enneagram-corner/enneagram-type-9) deserves a serious hearing.
findings.problem: The Type 9 and Type 2 alternatives sit at the end of a section titled "Love, accountability and the car keys". That section is about how he channels anger, so the turn to rival types feels like a detour. A reader scanning the headings for 'what else could he be' finds only "The case for Type 3" and could conclude that Nine and Two were never considered.
findings.acceptance_test: A reader who scans only the H2 headings can tell where the Nine and Two alternatives are weighed. Either the heading signals it, or the two paragraphs sit next to the Type 3 case. The anger-channeling section ends on its own point.

protected_passages.passage: So the question is whether the moral seriousness is the engine or the brand. This profile argues engine, with real dents.
protected_passages.reason: This is the clearest stakes statement in the piece. A reader who has never heard of him gets the central question in plain words and knows the article will be honest about counterevidence. It is the reason to keep reading.

protected_passages.passage: Haunted is a strong word for an ally to choose. It describes a gap between a standard and what one person can achieve, felt as a weight, which is close to the One's inner critic.
protected_passages.reason: This teaches the type through an outside witness's exact word rather than jargon, and in the next lines it names the limits (friendly witness, other types fit). A newcomer learns what a One feels like from a concrete detail.

protected_passages.passage: A failed child becomes a funding fight. A hospital bill becomes a price cap.
protected_passages.reason: A compressed, memorable statement of the pattern, earned by the two sourced stories just before it. An unfamiliar reader will remember this.

protected_passages.passage: A Three's nightmare is failing or being unseen. The one Talarico keeps describing is becoming the thing he fights, and he builds a rule in advance to stop himself.
protected_passages.reason: This makes the One-versus-Three discriminator concrete for a reader who knows no Enneagram. It is the article's main insight in two sentences.

protected_passages.passage: The One reading predicts he keeps the two-term pledge and keeps saying no to the next position. The Three reading predicts both soften in the spotlight.
protected_passages.reason: A testable ending that gives the reader something to watch after they leave. It turns the type argument into a prediction rather than a label, and it ages well.

assessment: As an unfamiliar reader I learn a lot and want to keep going. The engine-or-brand question is set up early. The sections build from origin to classroom to the quorum choices, then seminary, faith and anger, the Three case at full strength, and an honest list of what the read does not explain. The ending turns the thesis into a prediction. Type vocabulary is explained in plain language at first use. The weak point is orientation, not insight. The search description reverses the key fact. The hook relies on a quorum mechanic that is never explained, so the costliness of the return does not land. The 2026 race (Crockett primary result, who Allred is, Paxton over Cornyn) is never mapped, so the super PAC and allegation passages are harder to judge than they should be. A few connectives also point back to things the reader has not been given. All of these are cheap fixes that do not touch the argument. Similarity diagnostic: the tripped match ("the three types whose core emotion is anger", identical to the Daniela Amodei draft) and the near-match "Ones are driven by a need to be good" are standard type-definition sentences, which the command says are not evidence of formulaic writing. The Talarico-specific argument (quorum line, seminary, two-term pledge, 45 students, super PAC) is not reused, so I raise no distinctiveness finding. Rewording the definitional sentence would still be a costless improvement. I am escalating no new risks beyond those already in the evidence record: the single-source "mediocre" allegation keeps sensitive_allegations true, and medium-confidence One vs Three keeps contested_typing true.
